nature-gov-231.title: Fossil fuels: the energy we dig up
nature-gov-231.text:
In 2023, fossil fuels supplied 77% of world primary energy consumption and over 60% of electricity. A fossil fuel is a flammable carbon or hydrocarbon material formed naturally in the Earth's crust from the buried remains of prehistoric organisms. Coal, petroleum and natural gas are burnt for heating, to power engines and to generate electricity. Some are refined into kerosene, gasoline and diesel or turned into plastics and other petrochemicals. Because they take millions of years to form, they are non-renewable resources.

Burning them has negative externalities. Over 70% of human greenhouse gas emissions in 2022 was CO2 from burning fossil fuels, and that CO2 speeds climate change. They also release particulates, smog and acid rain. Air pollution from fossil fuels in 2018 was estimated to cost US$2.9 trillion, 3.3% of global GDP.

nature-gov-232.title: How buried life became coal, oil and gas
nature-gov-232.text: The energy in a lump of coal began as sunlight. Plankton that died and sedimented in anoxic conditions began forming petroleum and natural gas by anaerobic decomposition. Terrestrial plants tend to form coal and methane. Burial under sediment brought heat and pressure that turned organic matter into kerogen and then liquid and gaseous hydrocarbons. The energy released in combustion is still photosynthetic in origin.

nature-gov-234.title: Fossilflation: when fuel prices drive inflation
nature-gov-234.text: Economists have pointed to energy prices as the main reason for high inflation in 2022. Fossilflation is the impact of fossil fuel prices on inflation. Transport, food and shipping prices rise sharply when fossil fuel prices do. Mark Zandi says fossil fuel prices have driven every big inflation episode since WWII. Gernot Wagner argues commodities are volatile energy sources, whereas renewable technologies get relatively cheaper over time.

nature-gov-233.title: Health effects of fossil fuel pollution
nature-gov-233.text: Fossil-fuel air pollution was estimated to cause over 8 million deaths globally in 2018, nearly 1 in 5 deaths. The estimate was 10.2 million in 2019 and 5.13 million excess deaths in 2023. The harm comes from inhaling particulates and other air pollution from burning fuel. Effects include premature death, acute respiratory illness, aggravated asthma, chronic bronchitis and decreased lung function. The poor, the very young, the very old and those with respiratory disease are most at risk. Fossil fuels cause the highest greenhouse gas emissions and are the most dangerous to health; modern renewables appear safer and cleaner.

nature-hist-084.title: Pesticides: chemicals that guard the crop
nature-hist-084.text:
Farmers now use 3.73 million tonnes of pesticide active ingredient a year, a doubling since 1990. That was the figure for agricultural use in 2023, or 2.40 kg per hectare of cropland. Pesticides are substances used to control pests, including herbicides, insecticides, nematicides and fungicides. Herbicides are the most common, about 50% of all use worldwide. Most pesticides protect crops from weeds, fungi or insects.

Until the 1950s pesticides were inorganic compounds, such as copper, arsenic, mercury and sulfur derivatives, and plant extracts such as pyrethrum and nicotine. They are also used against disease vectors such as mosquitoes that transmit malaria, yellow fever and West Nile virus.

nature-hist-083.title: John Muir and the fight over Hetch Hetchy
nature-hist-083.text:
John Muir called sheep 'hoofed locusts'. He was a Scottish-born American naturalist and writer, called the Father of the National Parks, who championed preserving wilderness. His activism helped preserve Yosemite Valley and Sequoia National Park, and two Century Magazine articles shaped the 1890 act of Congress that created Yosemite National Park. He saw domestic sheep as the greatest threat to the Sierra. He co-founded the Sierra Club and served as its president until his death 22 years later.

Muir valued nature for its spiritual qualities. Gifford Pinchot saw conservation as managing resources for long-term sustainable commercial use. This split the movement into preservationists and conservationists. Both opposed reckless exploitation, but they clashed over damming Hetch Hetchy Valley: Pinchot called it the highest possible use, and Muir said to dam it was to dam a cathedral.

nature-hist-087.title: Alternatives to pesticides
nature-hist-087.text: Some farms fight pests without spraying. Alternatives to pesticides include cultivation practices, biological pest control, sterile insect release and genetic engineering of crops. Cultivation practices such as polyculture, crop rotation, timed planting and trap crops have controlled pests in some commercial systems while cutting pesticide use. Push-pull intercropping uses a crop that repels the pest and a boundary crop that attracts and traps it. Natural predators or parasites of pests can be released. Sterilised males can be released so mating yields no offspring, first used on the screwworm fly in 1958. Some evidence shows alternatives can be as effective as chemicals.

nature-hist-085.title: Pesticides: costs and benefits
nature-hist-085.text:
One study estimated up to $4 of crops saved per $1 spent on pesticides. Median yield increases range from 12% to 27% depending on the crop. Farmers gain from higher yields and a wider choice of crops, and consumers from affordable produce all year.

The costs fall on others. One study put annual US health and environmental costs at $9.6 billion, offset by about $40 billion of extra agricultural production. Over 98% of sprayed insecticides and 95% of herbicides reach something other than the target, including non-target species, air, water and soil. Resistance forces new pesticides or larger doses, which worsens ambient pollution, and cost about $1.5 billion a year in the US study. Use reduces invertebrate biodiversity in streams, contributes to pollinator decline and threatens endangered species.

nature-hist-086.title: How governments regulate pesticides
nature-hist-086.text:
Approval before sale is the usual rule. In many countries a government agency must approve pesticides for sale and use, and international codes seek common standards. Worldwide, 85% of countries have pesticide legislation on storage and 51% on disposal of obsolete pesticides.

The FAO adopted a voluntary International Code of Conduct on the Distribution and Use of Pesticides in 1985, updated in 1998 and 2002. In the US the EPA regulates pesticides under FIFRA and the Food Quality Protection Act, and registration can cost $50-70 million for one pesticide. The Stockholm Convention banned persistent pesticides such as DDT, which bioaccumulate in the food chain, so pesticides must now be degradable. A 2023 European Parliament committee decision aims to cut pesticide use 50% by 2030, and the most hazardous by 65%.

nature-hist-082.title: Global Forest Watch tracks forests in near real time
nature-hist-082.text:
A satellite-fed map helped tie the 2015 Southeast Asian haze fires to specific companies. Global Forest Watch is an open-source web application that monitors the world's forests in near real-time. Its fire data showed about 35% of Indonesian fires were in agricultural concessions, and its forest change data measure global deforestation rates and detect illegal clearing. Multinational companies use it to track supply chains against no-deforestation commitments.

It is an initiative of the World Resources Institute, with partners including Google, USAID, the University of Maryland, Esri and Vizzuality. It began in 1997 as a global forest monitoring network and was rebooted in 2013 using MODIS-derived data. The second version was released in February 2014.
